title: The Capital Phase in One Picture: Seat, Test and Date
summary: A checkpoint review of the capital phase as one system: every dollar has a seat in the stack, a test it must pass and a date it must be repaid. The same tests run at signing, during construction, in operation and at the exit, and one financing schedule keeps all three visible.
body:
The whole capital phase fits in one picture: every dollar in a project has a seat in the stack, a test it must pass and a date it must be repaid. If you can name all three for every dollar, you understand the phase; if you cannot, the gap is where the risk is.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between cross-default and cross-acceleration?

A. Cross-default treats another debt's default as a default here, even if that lender has done nothing; cross-acceleration applies only once the other debt has actually been accelerated.

Q. Why is the exit described as a second loan you do not yet have?

A. Because the construction loan is repaid by a permanent loan or a sale, sized to value and income at the time of refinance, in a market you do not control on the day you sign.

Q. What does a construction lender actually promise in a commitment letter?

A. To lend on stated terms only if every condition precedent is met by the stated dates; the promise is as strong as the conditions are achievable.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. This is a checkpoint week. For twelve weeks we have taken the capital of a project apart, piece by piece: the entity, the debt, the stack, the waterfall, the construction loan, pre-sales, project finance, country risk, stress tests, the exit and the post-mortem. This week puts the pieces back together. Today I give you the frame; each teacher this week returns to the hardest idea from their own seat. Nothing here is new; what is new is seeing it as one system.

Seat: who is paid first

In plain English: every dollar in the project sits somewhere in a queue, and its place in the queue decides its price and its risk.

The professional framing is the capital stack from Week 37: senior debt, mezzanine debt, preferred equity and common equity, in order of repayment. The senior lender is repaid first and so charges least; common equity is repaid last, takes the first loss and is paid for that with the profit. The intercreditor agreement sets the rules between the lenders, and the waterfall from Week 38 sets the rules between the equity partners. The entity from Week 35 is the box that holds all of it, and its resolutions decide who may sign for it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 50,000,000 dollar project: 30,000,000 dollars of senior debt, 7,500,000 dollars of mezzanine, 5,000,000 dollars of preferred equity and 7,500,000 dollars of common equity. If the finished building is worth 45,000,000 dollars, the 5,000,000 dollar loss falls first on common equity, which is left with 2,500,000 dollars of its 7,500,000; nobody else loses a dollar. If it is worth 40,000,000 dollars, common equity is gone and preferred equity has lost 2,500,000 dollars. The senior lender is untouched until value falls below 30,000,000 dollars. Seat decides who feels the first loss, and the first loss is always yours if you hold the common equity.

Test: what each dollar must pass

In plain English: every lender lends the smallest amount any of its tests allows, and keeps testing until it is repaid.

The professional framing is the binding limit from Week 36: loan to value, loan to cost, debt service coverage and debt yield, with the smallest answer setting the loan. During construction the test becomes the in-balance test from Week 40: undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete. During operation it becomes the covenant ladder from Week 44: cash trap, sweep and default. And at the end it becomes the refinance test from Week 45: the take-out, sized by the same three tests at the exit cap rate, must cover the balance plus costs. One family of tests, applied at four moments.

A second worked example. The same 30,000,000 dollar senior loan is tested at four moments. At signing, it is 60 percent of cost: it passes. In month 14 of construction, the monitor's cost to complete exceeds undisbursed funds by 1,000,000 dollars: it fails the in-balance test, and you deposit the gap. In year 3, NOI falls and coverage drops to 1.15 against a 1.20 trap: cash is held. At maturity, the take-out at a stressed cap rate is 28,000,000 dollars: you need 2,000,000 dollars more. Same loan, four tests, three of them failed at different moments. A developer who only checks the first test meets the other three as surprises.

Say that out loud now.

Seat, test and date: for every dollar, who is paid first, what it must pass and when it is due.

Date: when every dollar is due

In plain English: money has a calendar, and the calendar does not wait for the market.

The professional framing brings together the maturity gap from Week 45 and the maturity wall from Week 46. Each layer of the stack has its own date: the construction loan's maturity, the mezzanine's term, the preferred equity's redemption date, the investors' expected exit. When dates cluster, a closed market on one date can bring them all due together. When a date comes before the building can earn its exit, the plan fails on the calendar even if it succeeds on site. Pre-sale deposits from Week 41 and foreign-currency payments from Week 43 add dates of their own: the dates on which buyers must close and on which a hedge expires.

How the best do it

The most disciplined owners keep a single financing schedule for each project, maintained by the finance team and reviewed by senior management every month: one row per source of money, with its seat, its tests and their current values, its key dates and the person responsible. Problems are visible as a test approaching its limit or a date approaching without a plan, months before they are visible on site. A small developer can copy it with one spreadsheet tab and one rule: no financing is signed until its row is complete.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the character of each return, interest, preferred return, promote or fee, changes how it is taxed; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: guarantees and carve-outs connect the stack to your own balance sheet; each belongs on the schedule. Banking: lenders read covenant headroom and dates as a measure of your control; show them the schedule before they ask. Governance: every financing decision rests on a resolution of the right entity, signed by someone with authority. Estate: guarantees and positions in the stack outlive you unless documents say otherwise. Exit: every seat is repaid from the exit, so the exit decides whether any seat is safe.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's counsel on the full set of finance documents; accountant, on the financing schedule and its reporting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is understanding each piece and never seeing the system: a loan sized correctly, a waterfall written carefully and a guarantee negotiated well, which together fail because their dates and tests interact. The control is the single financing schedule, with seat, test and date for every dollar.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner learns the capital phase as vocabulary: stack, waterfall, in-balance, take-out. He can define each term and cannot say, for his own project, which test is closest to failing today.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. The financing schedule is a pre-mortem made permanent. Each row asks the question in advance: which seat loses first, which test fails first, which date arrives first.

Recap

Every dollar has a seat in the stack, a test it must pass and a date it must be repaid. The same family of tests runs at signing, during construction, in operation and at exit. Dates cluster into walls and gaps. Keep one financing schedule with all three for every source of money.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a stack that passed every test but one.
checklist: For every source of money, I can name its seat in the stack.
I know every test each lender applies and today's value of each.
I know the in-balance position at every draw.
I know every maturity, redemption and expected exit date.
No financing is signed until its row in the schedule is complete.
I know which test is closest to failing today.
I review the financing schedule every month.
head: Field checklist
speak: The capital phase fits in one picture: seat, test and date. Every dollar sits somewhere in the stack, senior, mezzanine, preferred or common, and its seat decides its price and when it takes a loss. On a hypothetical 50,000,000 dollar project with 7,500,000 of common equity, a 5,000,000 fall in value lands entirely on the common. Every dollar of debt must pass tests: loan to value, cost, coverage and debt yield at signing, the in-balance test during construction, the covenant ladder in operation and the refinance tests at exit. One family of tests at four moments. And every dollar has a date: maturities, redemptions, buyers' closings, hedge expiries. When dates cluster, a closed market brings them due together; when a date comes before the building can earn its exit, the plan fails on the calendar. So I keep one financing schedule with seat, test and date for every dollar, and I sign nothing until its row is complete.
terms: Financing schedule — one table listing every source of money with its seat, its tests and current values, its key dates and its owner.
Covenant headroom — the distance between a test's current value and the level at which a consequence is triggered.
First loss — the layer of capital that absorbs any fall in value before any other layer is touched.

hostile.q: You have explained every piece of your financing. Which part breaks first?
hostile.a: On today's numbers, the in-balance test during construction, because our contingency is the thinnest cushion in the schedule at about 4 percent of remaining cost. Next is the exit: at a cap rate one point above today's, the take-out falls about 2,000,000 dollars short, and that amount is held as committed equity. The coverage covenant in operation has the most headroom. I review those three every month, in that order.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on risk and the lender's view
title: The Stack That Passed Every Test But One: A Composite
summary: A composite case for the checkpoint: a developer sized every loan correctly and negotiated every document carefully, yet four guarantees, a personal in-balance deposit and an investor's control right combined into a channel from the building to his home. The seven steps show why the path of a loss must be traced before signing.
body:
This is a composite example: a developer who sized every loan correctly, negotiated every document carefully and still lost his own house, because nobody traced a single dollar of loss from the building all the way to his personal balance sheet.

Recall

Q. In the Week 46 reverse calculation, how much of the guarantee demand came from the costs of default itself?

A. About half: default interest, receiver costs and forced-sale costs, which is why the guarantor must act before default.

Q. What was the root cause in the Week 45 take-out composite?

A. A construction loan term shorter than the project's realistic path to refinance, combined with an exit sized at the going-in cap rate.

Q. What did the Dubai World standstill of 2009 show about default?

A. That a request to pause repayments on one obligation can spread to others through confidence and contract, so the reach of a default is wider than the loan it starts in.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman. Every case in this phase has had one main failure: a floating rate, a promote paid early, a peg that broke, a wall of maturities. Real collapses are usually several small, defensible decisions that connect. This composite is assembled from that pattern; the figures are hypothetical round numbers, and no real developer or project is described.

1. Timeline

Year 0: a developer starts a 50,000,000 dollar mixed residential project in a special purpose vehicle. Stack: a 30,000,000 dollar senior construction loan, 7,500,000 dollars of mezzanine debt, 5,000,000 dollars of preferred equity from an investor, and 7,500,000 dollars of common equity, of which the developer contributes 2,500,000. The developer signs a completion guarantee, a carry guarantee and a carve-out guarantee to the senior lender, and a smaller completion guarantee to the mezzanine lender. Month 18: costs run 6 percent over; the loan falls out of balance by 1,800,000 dollars; the developer deposits it from personal funds. Month 24: completion, three months late. Month 30: lease-up is slow, cap rates have widened, and the take-out appraisal is low. Month 34: the senior loan matures unpaid. Month 36: the senior lender calls the carry guarantee; the mezzanine lender calls its completion guarantee for cost items it says were not finished; the preferred investor exercises its right to take control of the vehicle. Month 42: the developer sells his home to meet the calls.

2. Key decisions

Each was defensible alone. Signing four guarantees to two lenders, each standard in its market. Funding the in-balance deposit personally, rather than calling capital from the investor. Accepting a preferred equity control right triggered by any senior default, including a maturity default. And not capping the carry guarantee in time.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed the vehicle limited his loss to his 2,500,000 dollars of equity. He assumed the guarantees were remote because the project was well underwritten. And he assumed each lender's documents could be read on their own.

4. Incentives

Each lender negotiated its own protection without regard to what the others had. The preferred investor's control right protected its 5,000,000 dollars but meant the developer lost the ability to manage a workout at exactly the moment workouts are decided. The developer's fee was paid at completion, and his promote depended on a profitable exit, so he was rewarded for optimism at both ends.

5. Warning signs ignored

The out-of-balance notice at month 18 was the first signal that the cushions were thin. Paying it personally hid the signal from the investors. Cap rates widening during construction were the second. The low appraisal at month 30 was the third, and by then three different parties held rights that could be exercised on the same date.

Say that out loud now.

The vehicle limits my loss only to the extent my signatures do not reach through it.

6. Point of no return

Roman places it at month 18. Once the developer funded the deposit personally, his personal liquidity was reduced at the start of the dangerous part of the project, and the investors had not been told the project needed more capital. Everything after that happened to a developer with less cash and less information shared than the problem required.

7. Root cause

The root cause was that nobody traced the path of a loss. Each document was sound. Together they formed a channel from the building's value, through the senior and mezzanine guarantees and the preferred control right, to the developer's home, and nobody had drawn that channel before signing.

The loss path, traced

Here is the trace he should have drawn. Suppose the building is worth 40,000,000 dollars at maturity instead of the 55,000,000 planned. Common equity is wiped out, including his 2,500,000 dollars. Preferred equity loses 2,500,000 dollars and takes control. The senior loan is covered by value, but it is not repaid on time, so the carry guarantee, uncapped, runs at roughly 2,400,000 dollars a year of interest until repayment. The mezzanine's completion guarantee is disputed and costs legal fees. The in-balance deposit of 1,800,000 dollars is already gone. Add it up: about 2,500,000 of equity, 1,800,000 of deposit, a year of carry and legal costs, perhaps 7,000,000 dollars of personal exposure on a project in which he believed his maximum loss was 2,500,000.

The same project with the trace done at signing: carry guarantee capped at twelve months of interest, cross-default narrowed, preferred control triggered only by the developer's own fault, not by a market maturity default, and a rule that in-balance deposits come pro rata from all equity. The loss is roughly halved, and the developer keeps control of the workout.

How to draw the loss path

Ford's method takes an hour and one sheet of paper. Write the building's value at the top, at three levels: plan, 15 percent lower and 30 percent lower. Below it, draw the stack as boxes, senior at the top and common at the bottom, and shade the boxes that lose money at each level. To the right, list every document that gives anyone a right on a default: each guarantee, each carve-out, each control right, each cross-default. Draw an arrow from the event that triggers it to the person it reaches. Then, at the bottom of the sheet, write one number for each value level: the total that could reach your own assets. If any arrow surprises you, the document behind it is the one to renegotiate. If the bottom number at 30 percent exceeds your liquidity, you do not sign until it does not.

Roman adds the lender's test: a sponsor who brings this sheet to the first meeting is negotiating guarantees from knowledge; one who does not is negotiating from hope.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reading each financing document on its own merits. The control is the loss path: a one-page drawing of how a stated fall in value moves through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to your own assets.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner pays a capital shortfall personally to keep investors calm. It drains the one cushion that belongs to him and hides the problem from the people who share it.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick taught the liquidity floor: cash you never spend, sized to survive your worst realistic month. This developer spent his floor on an in-balance deposit in month 18 and had nothing left when the guarantees came. Rule 7 and Rule 47 are the same discipline at two scales.

The prevention rule

Rule 47: Before I sign any financing, I trace one dollar of loss from the building through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to my own balance sheet, and I sign only if I can survive that path in the severe case.

Recap

Four guarantees, a personal deposit and a control right, each defensible, together formed a channel from the building to the developer's home. The trace, drawn at signing, would have shown it and cost little to change.

Next: JAX, on The Money: following gains and losses through the stack and the waterfall.
checklist: I draw the loss path before signing any financing.
I know every guarantee I have signed, to every lender, and its cap.
I know every control right an investor or lender can exercise, and its trigger.
I do not fund capital shortfalls personally without telling my partners.
In-balance deposits come pro rata from all equity, by agreement.
Control rights are triggered by my fault, not by market events alone.
I read every lender's documents against every other lender's.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer built a 50,000,000 dollar project with a senior loan, mezzanine debt, preferred equity and common equity, and signed four guarantees to two lenders, each standard on its own. When costs ran over, he paid the 1,800,000 dollar in-balance deposit personally, quietly. The building finished late, the take-out appraisal came in low, the loan matured unpaid, two guarantees were called and the preferred investor took control. He sold his home. His maximum loss, he believed, was his 2,500,000 dollars of equity; the real exposure was nearer 7,000,000. The point of no return was paying the deposit personally. The root cause: nobody traced the path of a loss through the documents together. Rule 47: before I sign any financing, I trace one dollar of loss from the building through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to my own balance sheet, and I sign only if I can survive it.
terms: Loss path — a drawing of how a stated fall in value moves through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to each party.
Control right — an investor's or lender's right to take over management or the entity when a defined trigger occurs.
Pro rata — in proportion to each party's share, so that a call for capital falls on all equity holders by their percentage.

hostile.q: Your project is in its own vehicle. Why should I believe your loss is limited to your equity?
hostile.a: You should not, and I do not claim it. Here is the loss path: at a 20 percent fall in value, common equity is lost, my carry guarantee is capped at twelve months of interest, the mezzanine guarantee is limited to completion items listed in a schedule, and the preferred control right is triggered only by my own default, not by a market maturity. My total personal exposure in that case is shown here, and my liquidity covers it.

rule: Rule 47: Before I sign any financing, I trace one dollar of loss from the building through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to my own balance sheet, and I sign only if I can survive that path in the severe case.

title: Two Queues: How Losses Climb the Stack and Profits Flow Down the Waterfall
summary: Every partner in a project holds a place in two queues: losses climb the capital stack from the bottom, and profits flow down the waterfall from the top. This checkpoint lesson follows one project through both, shows why a building sold above cost can still lose money for common equity, and sets out the founder health thread.
body:
Money moves through a project in two directions. Losses climb up the stack from the bottom; profits flow down the waterfall from the top. If you can follow one dollar each way through your own deal, you understand what every partner is really buying.

Recall

Q. What should you bring to the meeting after a guarantee demand?

A. Your lawyer, a sworn liquidity statement, counsel's analysis of the claim, an agreed proposal and walk-away number, and the discipline to stay silent after proposing.

Q. Name the four costs of a late exit.

A. Carry, fees, rate and proceeds, and the lost proceeds from a smaller refinance are usually the largest.

Q. Why do construction lenders usually require equity to be spent first?

A. So the borrower's money is at risk before the lender's, which protects the lender and tests the sponsor's commitment, at the cost of the equity being exposed for longer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, JAX here. Every partner in your project bought a position in two queues at once: a queue for losses and a queue for profits. Most investors read only the profit queue in the pitch. The best ones read both, and you must be able to show both, because a partner who discovers the loss queue in a downturn will never invest with you again. All figures are hypothetical round numbers; return levels and splits are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal.

Losses climb from the bottom

In plain English: the first dollar of loss is taken by whoever is paid last.

Take the stack from Monday: 50,000,000 dollars of cost, funded by 30,000,000 of senior debt, 7,500,000 of mezzanine, 5,000,000 of preferred equity and 7,500,000 of common equity. The finished building is planned at 60,000,000 dollars. Now walk the value down. At 50,000,000 the common equity has its money back and no profit. At 45,000,000 common loses two thirds of its money. At 42,500,000 common is gone. At 37,500,000 preferred is gone. Only below 37,500,000 does the mezzanine lose, and only below 30,000,000 the senior. The common equity, which includes you, holds the first 15 percent of value loss on its own. That is why it earns the profit.

A worked example of what that does to returns. If the building sells for 54,000,000 dollars after costs of sale, the senior and mezzanine are repaid with interest, the preferred equity gets its capital and its return, and what is left goes to common. Suppose debt interest and the preferred return absorb 6,000,000 dollars over the life of the project. Common receives 54,000,000 less 30,000,000, less 7,500,000, less 5,000,000, less 6,000,000, which is 5,500,000 dollars, against 7,500,000 invested: a loss of 2,000,000 dollars, even though the building sold above cost. The fixed claims ahead of you are paid whether or not you profit.

Profits flow down the waterfall

In plain English: once everyone ahead of you is paid, the common equity's profit is split between investors and sponsor by tiers.

The professional framing is the waterfall from Week 38: return of capital, a preferred return to the investors, often a catch-up to the sponsor, then a split. Suppose the building sells for 66,000,000 dollars net. After debt, preferred equity and the 6,000,000 dollars of carrying costs, common equity receives 17,500,000 dollars on 7,500,000 invested. The waterfall: first, 7,500,000 dollars returns everyone's capital, the developer's 2,500,000 and the investors' 5,000,000. Second, an 8 percent preferred return on the investors' capital over three years, about 1,200,000 dollars, simple interest for this illustration. Third, the remaining 8,800,000 dollars split 70 percent to investors and 30 percent to the sponsor. The sponsor's promote is about 2,640,000 dollars on top of its pro rata share. That is the reward for carrying the first-loss risk and doing the work.

Say that out loud now.

Losses climb from the bottom; profits flow from the top. Every partner owns a place in both queues.

Where the two queues meet

The two queues interact in three places, and each is a trap. First, the promote is earned only on profit above the hurdle, so a sponsor near the hurdle is tempted to take more risk to reach it; investors should ask what the sponsor earns in the downside, not only in the base case. Second, interim distributions of promote before investors are whole create the Week 38 problem: a promote paid on early gains and not recoverable when later losses arrive; a clawback must be backed by something real, such as a holdback of part of each promote payment. Third, fees paid to the sponsor, development fees or asset management fees, sit ahead of the common equity in practice even if they are not in the stack; the investors are entitled to see them in the same table.

How the best do it

Disciplined sponsors present the investor with both queues on one page: a value line from the severe case to the best case, showing at each level what every layer receives, including the sponsor's fees and promote. Investors see exactly where they lose and where the sponsor wins. A small developer can copy it with a table of five value levels and one column for each party.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Record your common equity at cost, not at the promote you hope to earn, and record the promote at zero until it is realised. Then record every guarantee and fee obligation beside it. The asset side of a developer's balance sheet is mostly hope; the liability side is mostly signatures. Keep them honest. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

Monthly thread: founder health

A checkpoint week is a reasonable moment to check the body as well as the knowledge. Debt stress is chronic, not acute; it shows in sleep, in temper and in the decision you make at the end of a long shift. Notice whether your sleep is worse in weeks when a maturity or a draw is near.

Treat a recurring pattern of poor sleep or persistent stress symptoms as information, and check that with your doctor rather than managing it alone. A developer's judgment is the most important asset in the stack, and it has no guarantee behind it.

A worked check on your own deal

Pick the value at which your own common equity breaks even, not on the building but on your cheque. In the example it is the value at which common receives 7,500,000 dollars back: 48,500,000 of fixed claims plus 7,500,000, about 56,000,000 dollars, only about 7 percent below the 60,000,000 plan. Most sponsors are surprised by how close that number sits to the plan. Write it in your investor pack beside the planned value, and investors will trust everything else in it more.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting only the profit queue, so that investors discover the loss queue in a downturn. The control is the two-queue table, with fees and promote, at five value levels, in every offering pack.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a building that sells above cost must produce a profit for common equity. Fixed claims, interest and preferred returns come first.

Callback

In Week 16, Sage warned about the difference between as-is and as-complete value. The two queues are only as good as the value they start from: build them from the appraiser's as-complete value, stressed, not from the pitch.

Recap

Losses climb from the bottom of the stack; profits flow through the waterfall from the top. Common equity takes the first loss and earns the promote. Show both queues, with fees, at five value levels.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: the phase's documents read as one set.
checklist: I can show what every layer receives at five value levels.
I know at what value my common equity is wiped out.
I include fees and promote in the same table as the stack.
Any interim promote is subject to a backed clawback.
I record my equity at cost and my promote at zero until realised.
Every offering pack shows both the loss queue and the profit queue.
I notice how deal stress affects my sleep and check patterns with my doctor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every partner holds a place in two queues. Losses climb the stack from the bottom: on a hypothetical 50,000,000 dollar project with 7,500,000 of common equity, the common takes the first 7,500,000 of any fall in value, then preferred equity, then mezzanine, and the senior lender is last. A building can sell above cost and still lose money for common equity, because interest and preferred returns are paid first. Profits flow down the waterfall from the top: return of capital, the investors' preferred return, then a split, which is where the sponsor's promote is earned. The traps sit where the queues meet: a sponsor near the hurdle tempted to take risk, promote paid early with no backed clawback, and fees that rank ahead of common in practice. So I show investors both queues, with fees and promote, at five value levels, and I record my own promote at zero until it is real.
terms: Fixed claim — a payment, such as debt interest or a preferred return, owed before the common equity receives anything.
Holdback — part of each promote payment retained to secure a later clawback.
Two-queue table — a schedule showing what every layer receives, including fees and promote, across a range of values.

hostile.q: Your pitch shows a 20 percent return. What do I get if the building is worth 15 percent less than you think?
hostile.a: Here is the table. At 15 percent below plan, the building is worth about 51,000,000 dollars; after debt, interest and the preferred equity, the common receives about 2,500,000 dollars of its 7,500,000, and I earn no promote. At 25 percent below, about 45,000,000, the common receives nothing, and my equity is lost alongside yours. I want you to invest knowing those numbers, not discovering them.

title: Six Documents Read as One Set
summary: The capital phase is governed by six documents: resolutions, commitment letter, loan agreement, intercreditor, guarantees and deposit trust. This checkpoint lesson reads them together with three questions, shows how one decision can need consents under several documents, builds a consent matrix, and compares Canada and Guyana on signing authority and security.
body:
The capital phase is governed by six documents, and the danger is never in one of them. It is in how they read together: who signed, what each lender may do, what each guarantee covers, and whose money is in trust. Read them as one set.

Recall

Q. What is a debt map?

A. A one-page picture of every loan, maturity, guarantee and cross-default and how they connect.

Q. Why might an extension option fail when you need it?

A. Because its conditions, such as notice inside a window and a coverage or debt yield test, are often set to the base case and missed in the downside.

Q. What is a condition precedent in a commitment letter?

A. A condition that must be met before the lender is obliged to fund, such as equity in place, permits issued or pre-sales achieved; until it is met, the promise does not bind.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, LEX here. Checkpoint weeks are for the ideas that cost most when you forget them. In law, that idea is simple: documents do not act alone. A lender's lawyer reads your guarantee against your loan agreement, your intercreditor and your resolutions; your lawyer must too. This lesson teaches concepts; verify every point against the primary source and with a lawyer licensed where the documents are governed before you rely on it.

The six documents

In plain English: six papers decide who controls the money and who pays when it goes wrong.

First, the entity's constitution and resolutions, from Week 35: who the company is, who may sign for it and what approvals a financing needs. Second, the commitment letter, from Week 39: what the lender promises and on what conditions. Third, the loan agreement, from Weeks 36, 39 and 40: covenants, draws, the in-balance test, events of default and maturity. Fourth, the intercreditor agreement, from Week 37: the rules between lenders. Fifth, the guarantees and carve-outs, from Weeks 40 and 46: what reaches your own assets and when. Sixth, the deposit and trust arrangements, from Week 41: whose money pre-sale deposits are and when they may be used.

Reading across: three questions

Read the set with three questions. Who may act? Who must be told? Who pays?

A worked example, hypothetical. The loan agreement requires lender consent to any change in the general contractor. The intercreditor gives the mezzanine lender a right to approve "material project contracts". The resolutions of the borrower require two directors to sign any contract above 500,000 dollars. The contractor becomes insolvent and you must appoint a replacement within two weeks. Reading each document alone, you need lender consent. Reading them together, you need the senior lender's consent, the mezzanine lender's approval, two directors' signatures, and probably notice to the guarantors under any guarantee that requires it. Missing any one may be an event of default, and the replacement contract may not bind the company if one director signed it alone. The time to know this is before the contractor fails.

A second example. A guarantee says the guarantor is liable for "all obligations under the Loan Agreement as amended from time to time". The loan is later extended at a higher rate, without the guarantor's signature. Under the general law in many places, a material change without the guarantor's consent might discharge it; the waiver language in the guarantee is designed to prevent that. Read alone, the extension is a lender and borrower matter. Read together, it has widened your personal exposure without your signature.

Say that out loud now.

Who may act, who must be told, who pays: I ask all three across every document, not inside one.

What to build

Build two short tools from the set. A consent matrix: a table of the decisions you will most likely need to make, such as changing a contractor, extending the loan, selling units below a price or admitting a new investor, against each document, showing whose consent, notice or signature each decision needs. And the covenant calendar from Week 45: every notice window, test date and final date across all six documents in one place. Together they turn six documents into one operating manual.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach two of these points. On signing authority, both countries' company laws generally let a company's constitution and its directors decide who may sign, and both have rules about when outsiders may rely on a signature, but the details of those rules differ and are set by statute and case law in each place [unverified — confirm independently]. On security over land, Canada registers mortgages under provincial land registry systems, with priority generally following registration; Guyana operates its own land registration and deeds systems, and the method of registering and enforcing a charge follows its own statutes [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical point in either place: a lender's security and your signing authority are only as good as their registration and approval. Verify against primary source before relying on either comparison.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, licensed in the governing law of each document and where the land sits.

The guarantor's checklist across the set

For each guarantee you sign, find four cross-references before signing. In the loan agreement: which events of default trigger the guarantee, and whether amendments need your consent. In the intercreditor: whether any lender's guarantee claim is limited the way its enforcement against the building is. In the resolutions: whether the borrower's signature on the loan was properly authorised, because a guarantee of an unauthorised obligation raises questions your lawyer must answer. And in the deposit trust: whether any use of buyers' money is a carve-out event that turns limited recourse into full recourse. Four questions, four documents, one guarantee. Do it once per guarantee and you will rarely be surprised by a demand letter.

What changes after signing

The set is not frozen at close. Every amendment, waiver, extension or consent letter is a seventh document that changes the other six. Keep them in one place with the originals, note in the summary what each one changed, and update the consent matrix and covenant calendar the same day. Many disputes in a workout turn on a side letter nobody had filed with the rest.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a decision taken correctly under one document and wrongly under another: a contractor replaced with the senior lender's consent and without the mezzanine lender's, a loan extended without telling the guarantors. The control is the consent matrix, prepared at financial close and updated with every amendment.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner keeps each document in its own folder, read once at signing by the lawyer who negotiated it. Keep a single summary of all six and read it before every significant decision.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct a lawyer: state the scope. A lawyer asked to review the guarantee will review the guarantee. Ask your lawyer, explicitly, to review the six documents together against a list of decisions you expect to make. That instruction is the cheapest protection in the phase.

Recap

Six documents govern the capital phase: resolutions, commitment letter, loan agreement, intercreditor, guarantees and deposit trust. Read them together with three questions: who may act, who must be told, who pays. Build a consent matrix and a covenant calendar, and instruct your lawyer to review the set, not one piece.

Next: Priya, on The Numbers: one project financed from land to exit, step by step.
checklist: I hold a one-page summary of all six financing documents.
I have a consent matrix for the decisions I am most likely to face.
I know who must sign for the company under its resolutions.
I know which decisions need the mezzanine lender's approval as well as the senior's.
I know which amendments need notice to, or consent of, the guarantors.
I keep one covenant calendar across all six documents.
I instruct my lawyer to review the documents together.
head: Field checklist
speak: The capital phase is governed by six documents: the entity's resolutions, the commitment letter, the loan agreement, the intercreditor agreement, the guarantees and the deposit trust arrangements. The danger is never in one of them; it is in how they read together. I ask three questions across all six: who may act, who must be told, who pays. Replacing a failed contractor may need the senior lender's consent, the mezzanine lender's approval, two directors' signatures and notice to guarantors. Extending a loan may widen my guarantee without my signature, because of the waiver language. So I build a consent matrix of likely decisions against every document, and one covenant calendar of every date. And I instruct my lawyer, explicitly, to review the six together, because a lawyer reviews the scope you give. Every point needs a lawyer licensed where each document is governed.
terms: Consent matrix — a table of likely decisions against each financing document, showing whose consent, notice or signature each needs.
Signing authority — the power, set by a company's constitution and resolutions, for a person to bind the company.
Registration — recording a mortgage or charge in the public register, which generally sets its priority and its effect against others.

hostile.q: You replaced your contractor last month. Show me the mezzanine lender's approval.
hostile.a: Here it is, dated before the new contract was signed, together with the senior lender's consent, the board resolution signed by two directors and the notices to both guarantors. We prepared the consent matrix at financial close for exactly this decision, so the replacement took nine days and did not create an event of default under any of the six documents.

title: One Project, Signing to Exit, in Nine Steps
summary: A checkpoint calculation that runs the whole capital phase on one hypothetical project: interest reserve, loan and equity, base and stressed take-out, a mid-build in-balance test, the effect of an overrun on return, the calendar against maturity and the rate exposure. The financing survives the stress, but the calendar and the rate must be fixed before signing.
body:
One project, financed from signing to exit, in nine steps. Size the loan to its tightest test, size the interest reserve, test the balance mid-build, size the take-out at stressed numbers and check the calendar. If every step passes, the financing works; if one fails, you have found the gap before the lender does.

Recall

Q. What are the seat, test and date of a dollar in the stack?

A. Its seat is its place in the order of repayment; its test is the sizing or covenant measure it must pass; its date is when it must be repaid or redeemed.

Q. How do you size a refinance?

A. By value, coverage and debt yield, taking the smallest, then comparing it with the construction balance plus closing costs, in a base and a stressed case.

Q. How did Week 39 test a construction loan's conditions and covenants?

A. Step by step against the borrower's own figures: equity first, pre-conditions met by their dates, and each covenant tested on the downside rather than the base case.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. In a checkpoint week the numbers lesson runs the whole phase at once. This is the page you should be able to produce for any project before you sign a construction loan. All figures are hypothetical round numbers; lending terms are commercial practice used for illustration, and real lenders set their own.

The facts

An apartment building. Land, hard and soft costs total 37,000,000 dollars. Construction takes 24 months; lease-up takes 9 months; the permanent lender wants 3 months of stabilised income before it closes. Stabilised net operating income (NOI) is forecast at 2,800,000 dollars a year. The construction lender offers up to 65 percent of total cost at 8 percent, floating, with a 36-month term. Today's cap rate for similar buildings is 5.75 percent.

Step 1: the interest reserve and total cost

Interest during construction is charged on a balance that grows as the loan is drawn. A simple estimate uses an average balance of about half the loan. Suppose the loan will be about 26,000,000 dollars. Construction interest is 26,000,000 times one half times 8 percent times 2 years, about 2,080,000 dollars. During lease-up the loan is almost fully drawn: 26,000,000 times 8 percent times 0.75 of a year is about 1,560,000 dollars, less about 600,000 dollars of NOI earned as the building fills, net about 960,000 dollars. The reserve is about 3,040,000 dollars; round it to 3,000,000. Total cost is 37,000,000 plus 3,000,000, which is 40,000,000 dollars.

Step 2: the construction loan and the equity

The loan is 65 percent of 40,000,000, which is 26,000,000 dollars, matching the estimate in Step 1. Equity is 14,000,000 dollars, spent first, as commercial practice usually requires.

Step 3: the base-case take-out

At stabilisation, value at 5.75 percent is 2,800,000 divided by 0.0575, about 48,700,000 dollars. A permanent lender at 65 percent of value offers about 31,650,000 dollars. The take-out comfortably repays 26,000,000. In the base case, the exit works with room to spare.

Step 4: the stressed take-out

Now stress the market: exit cap rate 6.5 percent and a permanent rate of 7 percent. Value test: 2,800,000 divided by 0.065 is about 43,080,000 dollars; 65 percent is about 28,000,000 dollars. Coverage test at 1.25: maximum debt service is 2,800,000 divided by 1.25, which is 2,240,000 dollars; the loan constant at 7 percent over 30 years is about 7.98 percent, so the loan is about 28,060,000 dollars. Debt yield at 9 percent: 2,800,000 divided by 0.09 is about 31,110,000 dollars. The binding limit is value, about 28,000,000 dollars. Against a balance of 26,000,000 plus about 280,000 of closing costs, the stressed take-out still works, with about 1,700,000 dollars to spare.

Say that out loud now.

The loan is sized at signing, but it is proven at the stressed exit.

Step 5: the in-balance test in month 14

By month 14 the equity of 14,000,000 dollars is spent and the lender has advanced 10,000,000 dollars, so 16,000,000 dollars remains undisbursed. The lender's monitor reports a cost to complete, including remaining interest, of 17,200,000 dollars, because the mechanical package came in high. Sixteen against 17.2: the loan is out of balance by 1,200,000 dollars, and you deposit it before the next draw. The question that matters is where the 1,200,000 comes from. Under the Week 47 rule, it comes pro rata from all equity, as the partnership agreement provides, not quietly from your own account.

Step 6: what the deposit does to the exit

The overrun does not change NOI, so the take-out is unchanged at about 28,000,000 dollars in the stressed case. But total equity is now 15,200,000 dollars, and the profit falls by 1,200,000. In the base case, value of about 48,700,000 less cost of 41,200,000 leaves about 7,500,000 dollars of profit on 15,200,000 of equity. In the stressed case, value of about 43,080,000 less 41,200,000 leaves about 1,880,000 dollars. The financing survives the stress; the return mostly does not. That is the honest distinction to give your investors.

Step 7: the calendar

Construction 24 months, lease-up 9, trailing income 3: the earliest take-out is month 36. The loan matures in month 36. There is no slack. A one-month delay anywhere puts the loan past maturity. Under Rule 45, you do not sign this as drawn. You ask for two six-month extensions with conditions calibrated to the downside, or a 42-month term, and you price the cost: perhaps a quarter point of margin, or an extension fee of about 0.5 percent, 130,000 dollars.

Step 8: the rate

The loan is floating. A one-point rise for the last 20 months adds about 26,000,000 times 1 percent times 20 twelfths, roughly 430,000 dollars, on a nearly drawn balance, against a 3,000,000 dollar reserve with no cushion. Either hold a cushion of about 500,000 dollars inside the reserve or buy an interest rate cap at closing. Write the decision down.

Step 9: the table

TestResultAction
Construction loan, 65 percent of cost26,000,000None
Base take-outabout 31,650,000None
Stressed take-outabout 28,000,000, value bindsHold; about 1,700,000 to spare
In-balance, month 14short 1,200,000Deposit pro rata from all equity
Calendarno slack at month 36Extensions or a 42-month term
Rateabout 430,000 exposed per pointCap or reserve cushion

All figures hypothetical, in dollars.

Step 10: the one-page answer for the lender

Turn the table into three sentences, because that is how the credit officer will repeat it to the committee. The loan is 26,000,000 dollars, 65 percent of cost, with 14,000,000 of equity first. The take-out works at a stressed cap rate and rate with about 1,700,000 to spare. The calendar needs slack and the rate needs a cap, and both are in the proposed terms. If you cannot say it in three sentences, you have not finished the nine steps.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is stopping at Step 3, because the base-case take-out looks comfortable. The failures in this project are in Steps 5, 7 and 8: the balance, the calendar and the rate. The control is to run all nine steps before signing and again every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sizes the interest reserve once and never re-runs it when the schedule or the rate moves. A reserve sized at signing is a guess by month 14.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage built sources and uses with a contingency sized to the estimate class. The month-14 overrun is that contingency being tested; a thin one at the pro forma stage becomes a deposit in construction.

Recap

Size the reserve and the loan, prove the take-out at stressed numbers, test the balance during the build, check the calendar against maturity and decide on the rate. Here the financing survives the stress, but the calendar has no slack and the rate is unprotected: both are fixed before signing.

Next: Roman, on The Room: a full mock credit committee for this project.
checklist: I size the interest reserve on an average balance in construction and near full balance in lease-up.
I size the construction loan and confirm it matches the reserve estimate.
I prove the take-out at a stressed cap rate and rate, by all three tests.
I know how an in-balance deposit will be funded before it is needed.
I separate whether the financing survives from whether the return survives.
I compare the earliest take-out date with maturity and require slack.
I decide in writing how the floating rate is protected.
I rerun all nine steps every quarter.
head: Field checklist
speak: One project, signing to exit, in nine steps, on hypothetical numbers. Costs of 37,000,000 dollars plus an interest reserve of about 3,000,000 make 40,000,000. At 65 percent of cost the loan is 26,000,000 and equity is 14,000,000. The base-case take-out, at a 5.75 percent cap rate on 2,800,000 of income, is about 31,650,000. Stressed at 6.5 percent and a 7 percent rate, value binds at about 28,000,000, still enough to repay the loan with about 1,700,000 to spare. In month 14 the loan is 1,200,000 out of balance, deposited pro rata from all equity. That cuts the stressed profit to under 2,000,000: the financing survives, the return mostly does not. The calendar has no slack: the earliest take-out is month 36, the same month the loan matures, so I need extensions or a longer term. And each point of rate costs about 430,000 against a reserve with no cushion, so I buy a cap or add a cushion before I sign.
terms: Interest reserve — a budget line, usually inside the loan, set aside to pay interest during construction and lease-up.
Average balance — the typical outstanding loan over a period of drawing, often estimated at about half the loan during construction.
Slack — the time between the earliest realistic take-out and maturity, which absorbs delay.

hostile.q: Your earliest refinance is the month your loan matures. Why should I approve that?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. I am requesting a 42-month term or two six-month extensions with a debt yield test calibrated to our stressed case. I will pay the extra margin or the fee, about 130,000 dollars, and I will buy a rate cap at closing so a rate rise does not exhaust the reserve during the extra months.

title: Mock Meeting: The Credit Committee for the Whole Phase
summary: A full mock credit committee for a construction loan, covering every part of the capital phase: seat, in-balance test, calendar, rate and personal exposure. The lesson gives the opening, the questions and model answers, the lines never to say, the hard closing question and two contrasting outcomes.
body:
The checkpoint meeting puts the whole phase in one room: a credit committee asked to approve a construction loan, with every question from seat to exit. Your job is to show you have already asked each question yourself, and to answer the hardest one before it is asked.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 47?

A. Before signing any financing, trace one dollar of loss from the building through every layer, covenant, guarantee and control right to your own balance sheet, and sign only if you can survive that path in the severe case.

Q. When a take-out appraisal comes in low, what do you say first to the lender?

A. The gap in dollars, with costs, unsoftened, followed by how much of it is time and how much is value.

Q. What is the first thing to negotiate in a commitment letter?

A. The conditions precedent and their dates, so that each is achievable on the downside, because the promise binds only once they are met.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here. A full mock meeting is the closest thing to the real committee you will face. Read it once as the developer. Then read it again as the credit officer, because the questions are the curriculum of the phase. The project is Friday's: hypothetical, 40,000,000 dollars of cost, a 26,000,000 dollar construction loan.

The scene

A lender's credit committee: the chair, the credit officer who has worked the deal, a risk officer and a junior analyst taking notes. You are given ten minutes to present and twenty for questions. The chair says: "We have read the memo. Tell us why this loan is safe, and then tell us what would make it unsafe."

The opening

Say: "The loan is 26,000,000 dollars, 65 percent of a 40,000,000 dollar cost, with 14,000,000 dollars of equity in first. It is safe because it is repaid by a permanent loan that works even if cap rates rise three quarters of a point and rates rise to 7 percent: in that case the take-out is about 28,000,000 dollars. It becomes unsafe in three ways, and I want to name them before you do: the in-balance test if costs overrun, the calendar if we are late, and the rate if we are unhedged. Here is what we have done about each."

Say that out loud now.

Why it is safe, what makes it unsafe, what I have done about each.

The questions, and the lines to say

The credit officer asks about the seat. "Who is behind us, and what can they do?" Answer: "Only common equity, 14,000,000 dollars, spent first. There is no mezzanine on this project. The partnership agreement requires any balancing deposit to be called pro rata from all partners within ten business days, and I have attached it."

The risk officer asks about the test. "What does the in-balance position look like if the mechanical package comes in high?" Answer: "Our own cost-to-complete forecast is reconciled monthly against your monitor's. An overrun of about 1,200,000 dollars on the mechanical package would put us that far out of balance in the middle of construction. The deposit would come from the partners under that clause, and we hold contingency of about 4 percent of hard cost on top."

The credit officer asks about the date. "Your schedule reaches stabilisation in month 33 and the take-out in month 36. That is the maturity." Answer: "Correct, and that is why we have asked for 42 months, or two extensions with a debt yield test set at our stressed case. We will pay for it."

The risk officer asks about the rate. "Do you have a hedge?" Answer: "We will buy a cap at closing at a strike that keeps interest inside the reserve. The cost is in the budget."

The chair asks about the person. "What do you personally guarantee, and could you pay it?" Answer: "Completion and carry, carry capped at twelve months of interest, both burning off at stabilised coverage. My combined guarantee exposure across all projects in a severe year is shown on page four, against my liquidity. I have traced the loss path; it is on page five."

The lines never to say

Never say "that will not happen" about any risk; the committee's job is to assume it will. Never say "the contractor guaranteed the price", because a fixed price is only as good as the contractor's balance sheet. Never call the take-out "committed" unless you have a commitment with conditions you can meet. Never answer a question about your own exposure with the vehicle's limited liability; the committee knows your signatures reach through it.

The hard question

The chair asks the one question every committee asks at the end: "If this goes wrong, what will we be sitting here discussing in two years?" Answer, without hesitation: "Probably a late lease-up in a higher-rate market, with the loan near maturity and the take-out smaller than planned. That is why the term, the cap and the stressed take-out are in the structure today, and why we will start the refinance twelve months before maturity and meet you the moment an appraisal comes in low."

When to stay silent

After the answer to the hard question, stop. The committee will look at each other. That silence is them deciding. Do not add a final reassurance; it dilutes the answer and signals doubt.

Holding your state

A committee of four asks fast and in turn, and the pressure is in the rhythm rather than in any one question. Slow it down: repeat the question in five words before answering, which gives you two seconds and shows you heard it. Keep the memo closed unless you need a number; reaching for paper reads as uncertainty. Kema's Week 4 practice, done parked before you walk in: three slow breaths, the outbreath longer.

Worked examples: two committees

Committee one. The developer presents the base case for ten minutes and is asked about the maturity in minute eleven. He has no answer, promises to look into it, and the committee approves on condition of a reduced loan of 23,000,000 dollars and a full repayment guarantee. He signs because time is short.

Committee two. The developer names the three risks in the first minute, shows the controls, asks for the longer term himself and answers the hard question in one breath. The committee approves at 26,000,000 dollars with the longer term, a capped carry guarantee and a condition that the cap is bought at closing. The difference between the two outcomes is about 3,000,000 dollars of loan and a guarantee he can survive.

After the meeting

Within a day, send the credit officer one page: the three risks, the controls, the requested terms and any commitments you made in the room, with dates. Then add the meeting to your decision journal: what you expected, what was asked that you had not prepared, and what you would change.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the committee find the weakness first. A weakness you name is a risk under control; a weakness they find is a reason to shrink the loan or widen the guarantee. The control is to open with the three ways the loan becomes unsafe.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner spends the ten minutes selling the building. The committee has read the memo; it wants to see the borrower think.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught bottom line first and the rule of three. The opening here is exactly that: one sentence on why it is safe, three ways it becomes unsafe, one action for each. The communication phase is how the capital phase gets approved.

Recap

Open with why the loan is safe and the three ways it becomes unsafe. Answer seat, test, date, rate and person with documents. Answer the hard question in one breath and then stay silent. Follow up in writing within a day.

Next: Kema, with the checkpoint: a mock interview, a recorded explanation scored on four measures, and the rules read aloud.
checklist: I open with why the loan is safe and the three ways it becomes unsafe.
I can answer for seat, test, date, rate and personal exposure with a document for each.
I name every weakness before the committee finds it.
I never call a take-out committed without a commitment I can meet.
I answer the hard closing question in one breath, then stay silent.
I repeat each question briefly before answering it.
I send a one-page follow-up within a day.
head: Field checklist
speak: At the credit committee I open with two things: why the loan is safe, and the three ways it becomes unsafe. On a hypothetical 26,000,000 dollar loan on 40,000,000 of cost, it is safe because the take-out works even at a stressed cap rate and rate. It becomes unsafe through the in-balance test, the calendar and the rate, and I show the control for each: a pro rata deposit clause, a longer term or extensions I am paying for, and a rate cap at closing. Then I answer seat, test, date, rate and person, each with a document, including my combined guarantee exposure and the loss path I have traced. I never say a risk will not happen, never lean on limited liability, never call a take-out committed when it is not. To the hard closing question, what will we be discussing in two years, I answer in one breath and then stay silent.
terms: Credit committee — the lender's internal body that approves or rejects a loan on the credit officer's recommendation.
Credit officer — the lender's analyst who works the deal, tests the borrower's numbers and recommends terms to the committee.
Strike — the interest rate level above which an interest rate cap pays the borrower.

hostile.q: If this goes wrong, what will we be sitting here discussing in two years?
hostile.a: Most likely a late lease-up in a higher-rate market, with the loan near maturity and a smaller take-out than planned. That is why the longer term, the rate cap and the stressed take-out are in the structure today, and why we will start the refinance twelve months before maturity and meet you the week any appraisal comes in low.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Capital, Debt and Project Finance
summary: Kema's checkpoint for the capital phase: a six-question mock interview with model answers, a three-minute recorded explanation of seat, test and date that you score yourself on four measures, and the rules you have committed to so far, read aloud and restated in your own words.
body:
The capital phase is learned when you can explain it under pressure, aloud, in three minutes, without notes. Today you find out whether that is true for every dollar's seat, test and date, and you write down the score.

Recall

Q. What are the nine steps of financing one project from signing to exit?

A. Interest reserve, loan and equity, base take-out, stressed take-out, the in-balance test mid-build, the effect of an overrun on return, the calendar against maturity, the rate, and the summary table with an action for each result.

Q. What is the exit card?

A. A one-page record of maturity, stabilisation, the take-out by three tests at stressed numbers, the refinance gap and its funded source.

Q. What did Week 39 teach about events of default?

A. That they are defined in the loan agreement, that some carry notice and cure periods and some do not, and that each one gives the lender the right to stop funding and enforce.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Kema here. Twelve weeks of capital have given you recognition: you know the terms when you see them. A lender's committee tests recall and performance. This checkpoint moves you from one to the other, and gives you a number you can compare at the next checkpoint. Progress you can measure is progress you can manage.

The mock interview

Read each question, answer it aloud before you read the model answer, then compare. Be strict with yourself.

Question 1. A lender offers 65 percent of cost. Why might you still get less?

Answer: Because the loan is sized by its tightest test. Coverage, debt yield or loan to value may bind before loan to cost, and at the exit the take-out is sized by value, coverage and debt yield at the exit cap rate. Worked check: 2,800,000 dollars of income at a 6.5 percent cap rate is about 43,080,000 dollars of value, so 65 percent of value is about 28,000,000.

Question 2. Your project sits in its own vehicle. What is your maximum loss?

Answer: My equity plus every guarantee, carve-out and deposit obligation that reaches through the vehicle, and any cross-default that brings in my other projects. I trace the loss path before signing; Rule 47.

Question 3. Explain the in-balance test in one breath.

Answer: At every draw, undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete, a forecast, not budget remaining; if it does not, the gap is deposited before the next draw.

Question 4. Your construction loan matures in month 36 and you can refinance in month 36. Is that acceptable?

Answer: No. There is no slack for any delay. I need a longer term or extensions with conditions calibrated to the downside, priced before I sign; Rule 45.

Question 5. You have guaranteed three projects. How do you test your exposure?

Answer: Not by expected loss, but by the combined call in a single severe year, because guarantees on projects in one market are called together. I compare that number with my liquid net worth every quarter.

Question 6. What did General Growth Properties teach?

Answer: That good assets do not refinance a maturity wall when the market is closed. Ladder maturities so no single year can force a sale, and survive a year with no refinancing; Rule 46.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Take out your phone, open the voice recorder and record a three-minute explanation of the capital phase as if to a new equity partner. Use this structure: seat, who is paid first and who takes the first loss; test, the binding limit, the in-balance test and the covenant ladder; date, the exit, the maturity gap and the maturity wall; and one failure case with its rule. Do not use notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Then listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow seat, test, date? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has done this many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you name your own personal exposure and the condition under which you would not sign, unprompted? A 5 raises the hard point before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. A worked example of honest scoring: if you stated the in-balance test correctly but said "budget remaining" instead of "cost to complete", accuracy is a 3, because that one word is the whole test. If you spent the first minute explaining what a mortgage is before reaching the stack, structure is a 3.

What to do with the scores

A score is only useful if it changes what you do next. Take your lowest of the four and act on that one alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson where the error came from and rebuild the definition in your own words. If structure was lowest, write seat, test and date on a card and record again tomorrow using only the card. If composure was lowest, record again deliberately slower and count filler words on playback. If the hard question was lowest, practise opening with it: "My maximum personal loss on this project is..."

Then record once more at the end of the week and compare with your recording from the last checkpoint. A move from 3 to 4 on one measure is real progress; a perfect score on the first attempt usually means the scoring was too generous. Keep every recording.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week. A rule you cannot say from memory will not be there when a lender is pressing you to sign before month end.

A worked example of a full recording

A strong opening sounds like this: "Every dollar in a project has a seat, a test and a date. I will take each in turn and finish with the rule I learned the hard way." Then one minute on seat, with the first-loss example; one minute on test, naming the binding limit and the in-balance test with the words cost to complete; forty seconds on date, the maturity gap and the wall; and twenty seconds on one rule. Time each part on playback. If one part ran twice as long as the others, that is where your understanding is still a story rather than a structure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading yourself on what you meant rather than what you said. The control is the recording: it does not care what you meant. Score the tape, not the intention.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the model answers instead of saying his own first. Reading gives the feeling of mastery without the evidence. The discomfort of hearing yourself explain the in-balance test is the rehearsal that makes the committee room feel familiar.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught "I'll confirm by Friday": never guess a number in a meeting. Listen for that on your recording. If you invented a figure rather than saying you would confirm it, mark accuracy down, even if the figure happened to be right.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud before reading the models. Record three minutes on seat, test and date without notes, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: Mr Shabazz, this is the checkpoint for capital, debt and project finance. Every dollar has a seat, a test and a date. Seat: who is paid first, and common equity takes the first loss. Test: a loan is sized by its tightest limit, during construction it must stay in balance against the cost to complete, in operation it meets a ladder of covenants, and at the exit the take-out is sized by three tests at a stressed cap rate. Date: the loan must not mature before the building can earn its refinance, and maturities must be laddered so no single year forces a sale. My personal exposure is my equity plus every guarantee that reaches through the vehicle, sized to the combined call in one bad year. Now record three minutes without notes, score yourself one to five on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and read your rules aloud.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of whether a phase can be explained and applied under pressure, not merely recognised.
Self-scored recording — a timed spoken explanation rated against fixed criteria so progress can be compared over time.
Recognition versus recall — the difference between knowing an idea when you see it and producing it unprompted.

hostile.q: You have studied capital for twelve weeks. In one minute, why should I lend to you?
hostile.a: Because I size every loan to its tightest test on the downside, I prove the exit at a stressed cap rate before I sign, I keep the loan in balance against my own cost-to-complete forecast every month, and I make sure the term reaches past my realistic stabilisation date. And I have traced how a loss would move from this building to my own balance sheet; I can survive it, and I will tell you the moment any test approaches its limit.
